name: ADF4002BRUZ-RL
title: ADF4002 phase detector / frequency synthesizer, 400 MHz RF input, 104 MHz PFD
summary: An integer-N PLL building block: a 14-bit reference counter, a 13-bit N counter fed by an RF input up to 400 MHz, a phase frequency detector up to 104 MHz and a programmable charge pump. With an external loop filter and VCO it closes a complete PLL; with R and N set to 1 it serves as a standalone PFD and charge pump. It runs from 2.7 V to 3.3 V, with a separate charge pump supply up to 5.5 V for a wider tuning range, and is set over a 3-wire serial interface. Uses are clock generation and conditioning and IF local oscillators.

circuits.title: Figure 21. ADF4002 as a PFD
circuits.description: With R and N both set to 1 the ADF4002 works as a bare phase detector and charge pump. The reference at REFIN equals the PFD frequency. CP drives a loop filter whose output tunes a VCO or VCXO supplied from VP. The oscillator output goes through 100 pF and an 18 Ω resistive three-way splitter: one arm, through a second 100 pF, is RFOUT; the other feeds an external prescaler that divides the oscillator down to the PFD frequency and returns it to RFINA through 100 pF, terminated in 51 Ω. RFINB is bypassed by 100 pF; RSET is 10 kΩ.
notes: CLK, DATA, LE and MUXOUT go to the serial interface; supply decoupling is not specified.
The loop filter is a block with no component values given.

circuits.title: Figure 20. ADF4002 as encode clock
circuits.description: A clean 77.76 MHz encode clock for an AD9215-80 12-bit ADC (up to 80 MHz encode). A 19.44 MHz TCXO is the reference; R = 1 and N = 4, the smallest multiplication, keep the ADF4002's noise contribution low. CP (pin 2) drives a loop filter that tunes a narrow-band 77.76 MHz VCXO, whose output returns to the RF input and clocks the ADC. The loop bandwidth is placed where the VCXO noise and the ADF4002 in-band noise cross. A 500 kHz, 1.8 V p-p generator through a filter is the ADC test signal; a PC sets the ADF4002 over SPI and reads the ADC FIFO board over USB. Measured rms jitter is under 1.2 ps, against the 6 ps rms the converter's 59 dB SNR allows.
notes: The SPI bus from the PC carries CLK, DATA and LE. Supplies, grounds, decoupling and the RFINB bypass are not specified.
The loop filter was designed with ADIsimPLL version 3.0.

circuits.title: Figure 22. ADuC812 to ADF4002 interface
circuits.description: An ADuC812 (8051 core) in SPI master mode with CPHA = 0 programs the ADF4002: SCLOCK to CLK, MOSI to DATA, and port pins for LE, CE and reading MUXOUT set to lock detect. LE is taken low, three bytes make each 24-bit word, and LE is taken high after the third. At the ADuC812's 4 MHz SPI clock the output frequency can change at up to 166 kHz. Any 8051-based controller can be wired the same way.
notes: P_LE, P_CE and P_LD are I/O port lines of the ADuC812.

circuits.title: Figure 23. ADSP-2181 to ADF4002 interface
circuits.description: An ADSP-2181 DSP drives the serial port into the ADF4002: SCLK to CLK, DT to DATA, TFS to LE, with I/O flags for CE and for reading MUXOUT as lock detect. Autobuffered transmit with alternate framing sends a whole block of words before an interrupt; the word length is eight bits, each 24-bit latch takes three stored bytes, and a write to the transmit register starts the transfer.
notes: FLAG_CE and FLAG_LD are I/O flag lines of the ADSP-2181.

operation.text: REFIN feeds a buffer through switches SW1 and SW2, normally closed, with a 100 kΩ bias resistor; SW3 is normally open. At power-down SW3 closes and SW1 and SW2 open, so the pin presents no load while the part is off (Figure 10).

RFINA and RFINB enter a differential stage, each biased at 1.6 V from a bias generator through a 500 Ω resistor (Figure 11). A two-stage limiting amplifier follows it and makes the CML clock that the N counter needs.

The 13-bit N counter (CMOS) divides the RF input by 1 to 8191 in the feedback path. The 14-bit R counter divides the reference by 1 to 16,383 to make the PFD reference. Output frequencies can be placed at steps of fREFIN / R.

operation.topic: Phase frequency detector and charge pump
operation.text: The PFD compares the R and N counter outputs and drives the charge pump up or down in proportion to their phase and frequency difference (Figure 13). A programmable delay sets an antibacklash pulse that removes the dead zone and lowers phase noise and reference spurs; ABP2 and ABP1 choose 2.9 ns or 6.0 ns. The shortest antibacklash width is not recommended. The PFD runs up to 104 MHz. With R and N at 1 the part is a standalone PFD and charge pump, for clock cleaning or a low-noise LO.

M3 to M1 in the function latch choose what MUXOUT shows: three-state, digital lock detect, N or R divider output, DVDD, open-drain analog lock detect, serial data out, or DGND. Digital lock detect is active high. With LDP = 0 it sets after three PD cycles in a row with phase error under 15 ns, with LDP = 1 after five; it clears when any later cycle has error over 25 ns. Above 10 MHz PFD frequency analog lock detect is the more accurate, its pulses being narrower. Analog lock detect is an N-channel open drain that wants a pull-up of about 10 kΩ; in lock it sits high with short low-going pulses.

Data enters a 24-bit shift register MSB first, one bit per rising CLK edge. When LE rises, the word moves into one of four latches chosen by its two LSBs, C2 and C1 (DB1, DB0): 00 R counter, 01 N counter, 10 function latch, 11 initialization latch.
CLK, DATA and LE form an SPI-compatible write-only port. The serial clock may run at up to 20 MHz, so a 24-bit word can be written every 1.2 µs, an update rate of 833 kHz.

F1 (DB2) at 1 holds the R and N counters in reset; it is 0 in normal operation. After power-up F1 must be written 0, and the N counter then counts in close alignment with the R counter, within one prescaler cycle.

CE low disables the part at once whatever PD2 and PD1 hold. With CE high, PD1 = 1 and PD2 = 0 power the part down as soon as PD1 is latched (asynchronous); PD1 = 1 and PD2 = 1 wait for the next charge pump event so the frequency does not jump (synchronous). In any power-down the DC current paths are cut, the R, N and timeout counters go to their load state, the charge pump goes three-state, digital lock detect resets, RFIN is debiased and the reference buffer is switched off. The input register still loads and latches data. Supply current in power-down is 1 µA typ.

Two charge pump currents can be programmed: current setting 1 (CPI3 to CPI1) for a settled loop and current setting 2 (CPI6 to CPI4) while the frequency is changing. F4 (DB9) enables fastlock and F5 (DB10) picks the mode. In mode 1 writing CP gain = 1 in the N counter latch switches to setting 2, and writing CP gain = 0 switches back. In mode 2 the switch back is timed: after the TC4 to TC1 timeout (3 to 63 PFD cycles) the CP gain bit clears itself and setting 1 returns. The timer counter works only in mode 2. A typical choice is 2.5 mA for setting 1 and 5 mA for setting 2; a new N written with CP gain = 1 then locks on the higher current for the programmed time.
F2 sets the phase detector polarity, negative at 0 and positive at 1. F3 at 1 puts the CP output in three-state; at 0 CP is active.

Written with C2, C1 = 1, 1, it loads the same bits as the function latch and also sends an internal reset pulse to the R, N and timeout counters and three-states the charge pump, so the N counter is at its load point when N data arrives and counting starts in close phase alignment. The reset pulse leaves the prescaler band gap and the reference buffer running. If the latch selects synchronous power-down, the pulse also triggers it. The first N counter load after initialization repeats the reset pulse; later N loads do not.

operation.topic: Programming after power-up: initialization latch method
operation.text: 1. Apply VDD. 2. Write the initialization latch (11) with F1 = 0. 3. Write the function latch (10) with F1 = 0. 4. Write the R counter latch (00). 5. Write the N counter latch (01). Four writes are needed after first power before the output becomes active.

operation.topic: Programming after power-up: CE pin method
operation.text: 1. Apply VDD. 2. Take CE low; the part powers down at once. 3. Write the function latch (10). 4. Write the R counter latch (00). 5. Write the N counter latch (01). 6. Take CE high; the R and N counters start in close alignment. Allow up to 1 µs after CE rises for the prescaler band gap and the oscillator input buffer bias to settle. Once programmed after VDD is applied, the part keeps its registers through CE power-down cycles, so CE can be used to wake it to check channel activity without reprogramming.

operation.topic: Programming after power-up: counter reset method
operation.text: 1. Apply VDD. 2. Write the function latch (10) with F1 = 1, holding the counters in reset. 3. Write the R counter latch (00). 4. Write the N counter latch (01). 5. Write the function latch (10) with F1 = 0. This gives the same alignment as the initialization method with direct control of the reset; while F1 = 1 the counters wait at their load point with CP in three-state, and no synchronous power-down follows.

operation.topic: Loop filter bandwidth for low jitter
operation.text: For lowest rms jitter of a VCXO-based clock, a bandwidth that is too narrow lets VCXO noise dominate close to the carrier and one that is too wide lets the ADF4002 noise dominate where the VCXO is quieter; the optimum is where the two noise curves cross.

Make each PCB pad 0.1 mm longer and 0.05 mm wider than the package land, with the land centred on it. The PCB thermal pad is at least as large as the exposed pad, with at least 0.25 mm clearance to the inner edges of the signal pads. Thermal vias, if used, sit on a 1.2 mm grid in the thermal pad, 0.3 mm to 0.33 mm in diameter, barrels plated with 1 oz copper to plug them. Connect the thermal pad to AGND.
